analysis.one_liner: Makes oil companies pay the full cost of offshore oil spills, ending a $75 million liability cap.
analysis.headline: The Senate environment committee approved the bill in August 2010 and put it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Weeks after the Deepwater Horizon blowout of April 20, 2010, this bill would have changed the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 so an offshore driller that causes a spill pays all cleanup costs and damages, instead of a $75 million cap (raised from the original $10 billion version). It would have shortened the time companies have to pay claims from 90 days to 30, required realistic worst-case spill response plans — including plans for a blowout — with field testing and public comment before approval, and required BP's claims fund to report to Congress on payments made.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently backstop spill costs beyond the $75 million cap; Gulf Coast residents, fishermen, and tourism businesses who would be fully and more quickly compensated for spill damages; and coastal environments protected by stronger, field-tested response plans.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million limit on an offshore facility owner's liability for a spill, so the responsible party — not the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund — pays all removal costs and damages.
Lets claimants go to court after 30 days instead of waiting 90 if their spill claim has not been paid in full, speeding compensation for people and businesses hurt by a spill.

Requires spill response plans to be field-tested, technologically feasible for the actual depth and conditions of the well, and to cover an uncontrolled blowout — the failure mode seen at Deepwater Horizon — with at least a 30-day public comment period before approval.
Requires the administrator of the BP claims fund to report to Congress on the fund's status and every claim paid, creating oversight of how spill victims are being compensated.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas producers and their insurers and guarantors, who would bear unlimited liability for spills and face stricter, costlier response-plan requirements — some of which could be passed to consumers through higher fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil drillers and their insurers

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability could make it difficult for some operators to insure deepwater drilling at all, potentially pushing smaller and mid-sized drillers out of the Gulf and leaving drilling concentrated in the hands of a few of the largest companies.

The bill applies retroactively, taking effect April 15, 2010 — days before the Deepwater Horizon explosion — so it would impose new unlimited liability on conduct that occurred before the law was passed.
Shortening the claim window from 90 to 30 days could pressure spill victims into accepting quick, incomplete settlements or into litigation they cannot afford.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — making polluters rather than taxpayers pay the full cost of a spill — is straightforward and was the direct response to a disaster whose damages ran into billions, far beyond the $75 million cap. The retroactive effective date is the weakest feature, and shortened claim deadlines and response-plan mandates add compliance costs that could reach consumers at the pump. On balance the benefits to taxpayers and coastal communities outweigh those costs, though the bill as reported was a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved it in August 2010 and it was placed on the Senate's general calendar, but the bill was never brought up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on May 4, 2010, weeks after the Deepwater Horizon blowout and explosion of April 20, 2010, initially raising the offshore liability cap from $75 million to $10 billion.

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee held hearings on June 9, 2010, ordered the bill reported favorably on June 30, and reported it with a substitute amendment on August 5, 2010 — a version that removed the liability cap entirely rather than just raising it.
Committee Republicans filed minority views against the bill as reported.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on August 5, 2010, and no further action was ever taken; it never received a Senate floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil producers kept the $75 million liability cap, leaving spill victims and the public fund to cover costs above it, and no stricter blowout-response planning requirements took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil drillers and their insurers

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 4, 2010, and led it through committee.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, moved the bill through markup, and reported it to the Senate with a substitute amendment on August 5, 2010.

against.name: Senate Republicans on the Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views against the bill when it was reported on August 5, 2010, and none of the 40 Senate Republicans cosponsored it.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the calendar in August 2010; no floor action occurred before the session ended.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed removing the $75 million liability cap on offshore spills.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the Senate's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and committee Republicans filed minority views against the reported bill.

industries.note: The bill removes the $75 million cap on their spill liability, making them pay every dollar of cleanup costs and damages — under current law the public fund absorbs costs above the cap, as happened after Deepwater Horizon. Their interest in keeping the cap runs directly against taxpayers and spill victims.

industries.industry: Insurers and guarantors of offshore facilities
industries.note: Guarantors of offshore facilities would face direct claims and unlimited exposure, since the bill lets claimants sue the responsible party or guarantor in court.

industries.industry: Oil spill response and remediation contractors
industries.note: Response plans would have to contract for regionally staged personnel and equipment sufficient to sustain a worst-case response, creating demand for response services.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: Full liability and faster claim payment would mean quicker, fuller compensation for the kinds of lost profits and livelihoods the BP spill inflicted on these industries.
